items.title: Shapes of alkanes and cycloalkanes (printed as a second 11.2.3)

source_refs.note: Shapes of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes (printed as a second 11.2.3) with Figure 11.4 and Tables 11.4 and 11.5, pages 249-251. Tables 11.4 and 11.5 are shown as original drawings of the printed tables.

blocks.text: The carbon atom in an alkane has four sp³ hybridized orbitals and forms four single bonds that are equidistant from each other Figure 11.4. Alkane molecules have a tetrahedral shape around carbon atoms.
Carbon atoms in alkane molecules form sigma bonds with surrounding carbon and hydrogen atoms.

As a result, carbon atoms in alkanes are surrounded by 4 pairs of bonding electrons which equally repel each other to form 109.5° bond angles and a C-C bond length of 1.54 Å. The shapes of organic molecules are generally represented using ball and stick formula. The shapes of some straight chain alkanes are shown (Table 11.4).

blocks.alt: Orbital drawing. Methane: four blue sp3 lobes spread from a central C, each ending in a yellow H; an arc between two lobes is marked 109.5 degrees; labelled sp3 hybrid tetrahedral. Ethane: two carbons, each with three lobes to H atoms, joined by two lobes that overlap end to end between the carbons.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.4: sp3 hybridised methane and ethane (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.4).

blocks.alt: Table with three columns: IUPAC name and molecular formula, structural formula, 3D structure. Rows: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10. Each displayed formula shows every C-H and C-C bond, with the carbons in a straight row and H above, below and at both ends. Each 3D structure is a ball-and-stick model with grey carbon balls and white hydrogen balls; the carbon chains of propane and butane are zig-zag.
blocks.caption: Table 11.4 Shapes of some straight chain alkanes (original drawing after the textbook's Table 11.4).

blocks.text: Cycloalkanes are cyclic, meaning that the carbon atoms of the molecule are arranged in the form of a ring. Cycloalkanes are also saturated, meaning that all of the carbons atoms that make up the ring are singly bonded to other atoms. The structural shapes of cyclopropane, cyclobutane and cyclopentane are shown below (Table 11.5)

blocks.alt: Table with three columns: IUPAC name and molecular formula, structural formula, 3D structure. Rows: cyclopropane C3H6 (triangle of CH2 groups), cyclobutane C4H8 (square of CH2 groups), cyclopentane with the formula printed C4H10 shown in red (five CH2 groups in a puckered ring). Each 3D structure is a ball-and-stick model with grey carbon balls in a shaded ring and two white hydrogen balls on each carbon.
blocks.caption: Table 11.5 Shapes of few cycloalkanes (original drawing after the textbook's Table 11.5; the formula in red is printed so in the book, see the correction below).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Cyclopentane has five ring carbons and cycloalkanes are CₙH₂ₙ, so its formula is C₅H₁₀; C₄H₁₀ is butane.
